items.readable_text:
Content:
Consider the differential equation
[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = e^{x - y}\,.]

Content:
The right-hand side is a function of both [MATH: x] and [MATH: y,] so we can't solve the equation by integrating both sides with respect to [MATH: x,] at least not straight away. So, how do we find a general solution to the equation?

Content:
First of all, note that it is possible to separate the variables [MATH: x] and [MATH: y] on each side of the equation as follows:
[MATH: (dy)/(dx) = e^{x − y} = (e^{x})/(e^{y})⟹e^{y} ⋅ (dy)/(dx) = e^{x}.]

Content:
Next, we integrate both sides with respect to [MATH: x,] and get

Content:
[MATH: ∫e^{y} ⋅ (dy)/(dx)dx|= ∫e^{x}dx.]

Content:
Using the rule for integration by substitution, we can simplify the integrand on the left-hand side and carry out the integration as follows:
[MATH: ∫e^{y} ⋅ (dy)/(dx)dx|= ∫e^{x}dx; ∫e^{y} ⋅ (dy)/(dx)dx|= ∫e^{x}dx; ∫e^{y}dy|= ∫e^{x}dx; e^{y}|= e^{x} + C.]

Content:
So, the general solution to the differential equation is

Content:
[MATH: e^y = e^x + C.]

Content:
This is an implicit form of the solution since it is not written explicitly as [MATH: y=y(x).]

Content:
We can write our general solution in explicit form (i.e., in the form [MATH: y=y(x)]) by noting that since [MATH: e^y > 0] for all [MATH: y], we may assume that the right-hand side is positive and apply the natural logarithm, as follows:
[MATH: \ln (e^{y})|= \ln (e^{x} + C); y|= \ln (e^{x} + C)]

sections.normalized_html:
Given that [MATH: x,y \geq 0,] separate the variables in the following differential equation:

[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = \sqrt{2xy}]

[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = \sqrt{2xy}]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
A differentiable equation is separable if it can be written in the form

[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = h(x)g(y).]

If an equation is separable, we say that the variables are separated when it is written in the form

[MATH: \dfrac{1}{g(y)} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = h(x).]

Notice that our differentiable equation is separable since it can be written as

[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = \sqrt{2x} \cdot \sqrt{y}.]

Therefore, we separate the variables as follows:

[MATH: \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{y}} \cdot \dfrac {\textrm{d}y} {\textrm{d}x} = \sqrt{2x}]

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to [MATH: x{:}] [MATH: ∫y(dy)/(dx)dx|= ∫x^{2}dx; ∫y(dy)/(dx)dx|= ∫x^{2}dx; ∫ydy|= ∫x^{2}dx; (1)/(2)y^{2}|= (1)/(3)x^{3} + C]

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is [MATH: \dfrac{1}{2}y^2 = \dfrac{1}{3}x^3 + C.]

We can express the solution in the form [MATH: y = y(x)] as follows:

[MATH: (1)/(2)y^{2}|= (1)/(3)x^{3} + C; y^{2}|= (2)/(3)x^{3} + 2C; y|= ± sqrt((2)/(3)x^{3} + 2C); y|= ± sqrt((2)/(3)x^{3} + K)] where [MATH: K = 2C.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables: [MATH: y^{′} + 2xy|= 0; (dy)/(dx) + 2xy|= 0; (dy)/(dx)|= − 2xy; (1)/(y) ⋅ (dy)/(dx)|= − 2x]

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to [MATH: x{:}] [MATH: ∫(1)/(y) ⋅ (dy)/(dx)dx|= ∫(− 2x)dx; ∫(1)/(y)dy|= − 2∫xdx; \ln|y||= − x^{2} + C]

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is [MATH: \ln \vert y \vert = -x^2 + C.]

We're required to write the solution in the form [MATH: y = y(x).] By doing this, we get [MATH: \ln|y||= − x^{2} + C;|y||= e^{− x^{2} + C};|y||= e^{− x^{2}} ⋅ e^{C};|y||= Ke^{− x^{2}}] where [MATH: K = e^C] and [MATH: K > 0.]

We can drop the absolute value bars by allowing [MATH: K] to be either positive or negative. Therefore, the most general solution is [MATH: y = Ke^{-x^2}.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Consider the differential equation
[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = e^{x - y}\,.]

Content:
The right-hand side is a function of both [MATH: x] and [MATH: y,] so we can't solve the equation by integrating both sides with respect to [MATH: x,] at least not straight away. So, how do we find a general solution to the equation?

Content:
First of all, note that it is possible to separate the variables [MATH: x] and [MATH: y] on each side of the equation as follows:
[MATH: (dy)/(dx) = e^{x − y} = (e^{x})/(e^{y})⟹e^{y} ⋅ (dy)/(dx) = e^{x}.]

Content:
Next, we integrate both sides with respect to [MATH: x,] and get

Content:
[MATH: ∫e^{y} ⋅ (dy)/(dx)dx|= ∫e^{x}dx.]

Content:
Using the rule for integration by substitution, we can simplify the integrand on the left-hand side and carry out the integration as follows:
[MATH: ∫e^{y} ⋅ (dy)/(dx)dx|= ∫e^{x}dx; ∫e^{y} ⋅ (dy)/(dx)dx|= ∫e^{x}dx; ∫e^{y}dy|= ∫e^{x}dx; e^{y}|= e^{x} + C.]

Content:
So, the general solution to the differential equation is

Content:
[MATH: e^y = e^x + C.]

Content:
This is an implicit form of the solution since it is not written explicitly as [MATH: y=y(x).]

Content:
We can write our general solution in explicit form (i.e., in the form [MATH: y=y(x)]) by noting that since [MATH: e^y > 0] for all [MATH: y], we may assume that the right-hand side is positive and apply the natural logarithm, as follows:
[MATH: \ln (e^{y})|= \ln (e^{x} + C); y|= \ln (e^{x} + C)]

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: First-Order Separable Equations

Content:
The differential equation that we just solved was separable. A first-order differential equation is separable if it can be written in the form
[MATH: \dfrac {\textrm{d}y} {\textrm{d}x} = h(x)g(y).]

Content:
If an equation is separable, we say that the variables are separated when it is written in the form

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{1}{g(y)} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = h(x).]

Content:
Once the variables are separated, we can integrate both sides of the equation with respect to [MATH: x,] as follows:
[MATH: ∫(1)/(g(y)) ⋅ (dy)/(dx)dx|= ∫h(x)dx; ∫(dy)/(g(y))|= ∫h(x)dx.]
We then evaluate both integrals and find the solution. Note that for the solution to be valid, we require [MATH: g(y)\neq 0.]

---

Item 3 — Example: Separating the Variables in a Differential Equation

Example Prompt:
Given that [MATH: x,y \geq 0,] separate the variables in the following differential equation:

[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = \sqrt{2xy}]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
A differentiable equation is separable if it can be written in the form

[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = h(x)g(y).]

If an equation is separable, we say that the variables are separated when it is written in the form

[MATH: \dfrac{1}{g(y)} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = h(x).]

Notice that our differentiable equation is separable since it can be written as

[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = \sqrt{2x} \cdot \sqrt{y}.]

Therefore, we separate the variables as follows:

[MATH: \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{y}} \cdot \dfrac {\textrm{d}y} {\textrm{d}x} = \sqrt{2x}]

---

Item 6 — Example: Finding a General Solution in Implicit Form

Example Prompt:
Find the general solution to the differential equation [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}
=
\dfrac{x}{y}.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

[MATH: (dy)/(dx)|= (x)/(y); y(dy)/(dx)|= x]

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to [MATH: x{:}]
[MATH: ∫y(dy)/(dx)dx|= ∫xdx; ∫y(dy)/(dx)dx|= ∫xdx; ∫ydy|= ∫xdx; (y^{2})/(2)|= (x^{2})/(2) + K; y^{2}|= x^{2} + 2K; y^{2}|= x^{2} + C,]
where [MATH: C= 2K.]

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

[MATH: y^2 = x^2 + C .]

Item 9 — Example: Finding a General Solution in Explicit Form

Example Prompt:
Find the general solution to the differential equation [MATH: y' = \dfrac {x^2}{y}.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:
[MATH: y^{′}|= (x^{2})/(y); (dy)/(dx)|= (x^{2})/(y); y(dy)/(dx)|= x^{2}]

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to [MATH: x{:}]
[MATH: ∫y(dy)/(dx)dx|= ∫x^{2}dx; ∫y(dy)/(dx)dx|= ∫x^{2}dx; ∫ydy|= ∫x^{2}dx; (1)/(2)y^{2}|= (1)/(3)x^{3} + C]

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is
[MATH: \dfrac{1}{2}y^2 = \dfrac{1}{3}x^3 + C.]

We can express the solution in the form [MATH: y = y(x)] as follows:

[MATH: (1)/(2)y^{2}|= (1)/(3)x^{3} + C; y^{2}|= (2)/(3)x^{3} + 2C; y|= ± sqrt((2)/(3)x^{3} + 2C); y|= ± sqrt((2)/(3)x^{3} + K)]
where [MATH: K = 2C.]

Item 12 — Example: Finding General Solutions by Rearranging Then Integrating

Example Prompt:
Find the general solution to the differential equation [MATH: y' + 2xy = 0] for [MATH: y\neq 0.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:
[MATH: y^{′} + 2xy|= 0; (dy)/(dx) + 2xy|= 0; (dy)/(dx)|= − 2xy; (1)/(y) ⋅ (dy)/(dx)|= − 2x]

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to [MATH: x{:}]
[MATH: ∫(1)/(y) ⋅ (dy)/(dx)dx|= ∫(− 2x)dx; ∫(1)/(y)dy|= − 2∫xdx; \ln|y||= − x^{2} + C]

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is
[MATH: \ln \vert y \vert = -x^2 + C.]

We're required to write the solution in the form [MATH: y = y(x).] By doing this, we get
[MATH: \ln|y||= − x^{2} + C;|y||= e^{− x^{2} + C};|y||= e^{− x^{2}} ⋅ e^{C};|y||= Ke^{− x^{2}}]
where [MATH: K = e^C] and [MATH: K > 0.]

We can drop the absolute value bars by allowing [MATH: K] to be either positive or negative. Therefore, the most general solution is
[MATH: y = Ke^{-x^2}.]
